en: The Theravāda Vinaya Mahāvibhaṅga:
The Section on Offenses Entailing Expiation (Pācittiyakaṇḍa)
Sahadhammika-vagga 76.
The Training Rule on Groundless Accusations.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, the group-of-six bhikkhus groundlessly charged a bhikkhu with an offense entailing suspension (*saṅghādisesa*).
Those bhikkhus who were of few desires... [and so on]... complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
"How can the group-of-six bhikkhus groundlessly charge a bhikkhu with an offense entailing suspension?"... [and so on].
“Is it true, monks, that you groundlessly charged a monk with an offense entailing suspension?
“It is true, Blessed One.
The Buddha, the Blessed One, rebuked them... [as before]...
"How indeed, you foolish men, can you groundlessly charge a bhikkhu with a *saṅghādisesa* offense?
This, foolish men, does not lead to the confidence of those without confidence...
And furthermore, monks, you should recite this training rule as follows:"
“Whatever bhikkhu should groundlessly charge another bhikkhu with an offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa), it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
“Whatever bhikkhu” means whichever such person... [etc.]
“Bhikkhu” … [as before] … this is the “bhikkhu” intended in this context. “Bhikkhunī” … [as before] … this is the “bhikkhunī” intended in this context.
Another monk.
"Groundless" means not seen,
not heard, and not suspected.
"By a *saṅghādisesa*" means by any one of the thirteen.
"Should accuse" means:
If one accuses or causes another to accuse [a person], there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
If one accuses a person who is fully ordained, perceiving them as fully ordained, with a groundless *saṅghādisesa* offense, there is an offense of expiation.
If one accuses a person who is fully ordained, being uncertain [of their status], with a groundless *saṅghādisesa* offense, there is an offense of expiation.
If one who is fully ordained, perceiving another as not fully ordained, charges them with a groundless *saṅghādisesa* offense, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*).
If one charges them on account of a failure in conduct or a failure in view, there is an offense of wrong-doing (*dukkaṭa*).
If one charges one who is not fully ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If [the person] is not ordained, but one perceives them as ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing (dukkaṭa).
If [the person] is not ordained, but one is doubtful, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
If [the person] is not ordained, and one perceives them as not ordained, there is an offense of wrong-doing.
There is no offense if one accuses or causes another to accuse while perceiving it to be so,
or in the case of one who is insane.
"For one who is a first-offender":
the sixth training rule concerning groundless charges is concluded.
